The most tempting rejection in the chapter and the reason this register exists. “so as by fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 1 Corinthians 3:15, “he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire” — and Ether 4:9 ends “the inhabitants thereof shall pass away, even so as by fire”. A four-word King James singleton reproduced with one word changed is normally decisive evidence, and here it is not, because the two verses use the fire for opposite purposes. Paul's fire tries a man's work, destroys the work, and lets the man through; the adverbial “yet” is doing the whole job, conceding a loss in order to affirm a salvation. Ether 4:9's fire is the instrument by which the inhabitants of the earth are removed, and its “even” intensifies a threat rather than qualifying a rescue. Nothing else of 1 Corinthians 3 is anywhere near this verse — no builders, no foundation, no gold and stubble, no day that declares it — and Ether 4:9's three clauses are otherwise a catalogue of cosmic authority (heavens opened and shut, earth shaken) with no soteriology in them at all. The machine matched “that i am and” against “I AM THAT I AM: and”, and the temptation is real, because Ether 4:12 is a chain of divine self-predications (“I am the Father, I am the light, and the life”) and Exodus 3:14 is the one KJV verse where the divine name is a self-predication. But the shared words are not doing the same work. In Ether 4:12 “that I am” is the object of a verb of believing — “he that will not believe me, that I am” — an ellipsis for believing in the speaker's existence or identity; in Exodus 3:14 “THAT” is a relative and the phrase is a name given to Moses to repeat. The Book of Mormon's absolute “I am” self-predications in this verse are Johannine in form (see the John 14:6 row), not Mosaic, and the chapter shows no other contact with the burning bush.

“For good cometh of none, save it be of me” states in the Lord's own voice what Mark 10:18 and Matthew 19:17 state as a question — “Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God”. The proposition is the same and the phrase “none good but one” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both of them that saying. It is excluded on two counts. There is no shared distinctive wording at all: “none” and “good” are the only common words and their syntax differs entirely. And the sense is inverted at the point that matters most — the synoptic saying deflects the title away from the speaker, and Ether 4:12 claims it for him. A Book of Mormon verse in which Christ says that all good comes of him is doing the opposite of the verse in which Christ declines to be called good. Recorded because a reader who knows the synoptic saying will think of it here.

“The knowledge which is hid up because of unbelief” invites Colossians 2:3, “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”, and “the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Two words in common is not enough, and the two hidings are of different kinds: Paul's knowledge is hidden *in Christ* as a location, permanently and by nature, while Ether 4:13's is hidden *from* a people, contingently, and released on repentance. The concealment language in this passage is adjudicated two verses later, at 4:15, where “hid up from the foundation of the world” has a real KJV background in Matthew 13:35's “kept secret from the foundation of the world” — a hiding that is likewise a withholding from those who will not receive, and that carries the parable theory the chapter is working with. A reader at 4:13 is sent there.

A five-word run scoring 2.00 across a clause boundary, and every word of it is connective. Ether 4:15's “...from the foundation of the world from you; yea, when ye shall call upon the Father” and Isaiah 1:15's “I will hide mine eyes from you: yea, when ye make many prayers” happen to place the same three particles in the same order. There is a faint thematic overlap — both concern prayer that God will or will not hear — but Isaiah 1:15 refuses the prayers of bloody hands and Ether 4:15 promises to hear the broken-hearted, and the resemblance does not survive the second clause. A textbook case of the n-gram stream scoring rare boilerplate (CONVENTIONS §9).
